In adults with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction, what is the hazard of a first cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization with sacubitril/valsartan compared with enalapril?

Contents
Abstract

Background. Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition changed the treatment of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction on the strength of a single large trial. Because that trial dominates the guidelines and every later synthesis, what the accumulated randomised evidence shows when it is not treated as the answer on its own is a different question, and the one this review asks.

Methods. PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched on 2026-08-12 with no language, date or publication-status filter. Randomised trials of sacubitril/valsartan against enalapril in adults with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction were eligible if they reported the composite of cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure as a time-to-first-event hazard ratio. Hazard ratios were pooled on the log scale by generic inverse variance under a random-effects model with the REML estimator. Risk of bias used the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials, effect-of-assignment variant, assessed independently by two assessors. Certainty used the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach.

Results. 423 records were screened and 4 trials contributing 9,734 randomised participants met all eligibility conditions. The pooled hazard ratio was 0.872 (0.746 to 1.02), an interval that includes no effect. Heterogeneity was moderate and estimator-dependent, with I-squared 32.9 percent under the registered estimator. The pooled result is dominated by one trial: omitting the largest gives 0.966 (0.79 to 1.18), and each of the three remaining trials has an interval that includes no effect. No risk-of-bias domain was rated high. Certainty was low.

Conclusions. Across 4 randomised trials the pooled estimate is compatible with no difference between sacubitril/valsartan and enalapril for a first cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation. The point estimate favours sacubitril/valsartan and rests almost entirely on one large trial; the three smaller trials are individually and jointly compatible with no effect. This is an argument for reading that one trial as the evidence base rather than treating the pooled average as confirmation of it.
Introduction

Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction carries a mortality and rehospitalisation burden that renin-angiotensin system inhibition reduces but does not remove. Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition was developed to act on a second pathway at the same time, combining neprilysin inhibition, which raises natriuretic peptide concentrations, with angiotensin receptor blockade.

The pivotal comparison against enalapril reported a substantial reduction in the composite of cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation and was stopped early by prespecified rule for overwhelming benefit. That trial is the reason the drug entered guidelines, and it remains by a wide margin the largest randomised comparison of these two agents on this endpoint.

Three later randomised comparisons against the same active comparator have reported the same composite in different populations. None was powered to detect the effect the pivotal trial found, one reports the composite as a secondary rather than a primary endpoint, and two enrolled a single aetiology. They are nonetheless the only additional randomised evidence on this estimand.

A meta-analysis in which one trial contributes most of the information is often criticised as adding nothing to that trial. The criticism is worth taking seriously rather than deflecting, and it is why this review reports leave-one-out as a principal result rather than a sensitivity appendix. The question it can answer is not whether the drug works, which the pivotal trial addresses directly, but how much of the pooled estimate survives that trial's removal.
Methods
Protocol and registration

The protocol was registered before any query was executed, as a timestamped commit in a public repository, and is reachable at a SHA-pinned permalink that cannot be rewritten without changing the hash. The interval between registration and the first executed query was +51 min 31 s to the attempt, +54 min 52 s to the first successful execution, and the ordering is re-tested at every build rather than asserted once. Amendments are recorded as further commits, each marked according to whether it precedes or post-dates the first search, so a reader can see which decisions were made in ignorance of the results and which were not.
Eligibility criteria

Trials were eligible if they randomised adults with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction to sacubitril/valsartan or to enalapril and reported the composite of cardiovascular death or first heart failure hospitalisation as a time-to-first-event hazard ratio. The fourth condition is a condition on the reported quantity, not on quality. Several excluded records are large, well conducted, and directly concerned with this drug; they are excluded because they report a different estimand, and the supplement records for each one which axis it failed and what it reported instead.
Information sources and search

PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched on 2026-08-12. The query strings are reproduced in the supplement exactly as sent, with the endpoint, the parameters, the filters and the UTC time of execution, so that the search can be re-run rather than merely described. No language, date or publication-status filter was applied. 423 records were returned and every one is listed with its disposition.
Study selection and data collection

Records were screened against the eligibility axes, and each exclusion records the axis that failed and, where the failure was on a reported quantity, the quantity the record gave instead. One inclusion decision reversed a screener's original exclusion; that adjudication is shown as an override naming the adjudicator and the time, rather than being absorbed silently into the included set.
Effect measures and synthesis

Hazard ratios were analysed on the log scale by generic inverse variance, with the standard error implied by each published interval. A random-effects model was fitted with the REML estimator of the between-study variance; DerSimonian-Laird was not used, because it is known to be biased when the number of trials is small, and with 4 trials that condition holds. Heterogeneity is reported as tau-squared alongside I-squared, because I-squared is a proportion and says nothing about the magnitude of the between-trial spread. Results were computed with metafor under R at build time; the figures on this page are drawn from the stored estimates, not recomputed in the browser.
Risk of bias

Each pooled result was assessed with RoB-2 using the effect-of-assignment variant, at the level of the result being pooled rather than the trial overall. Two assessors worked independently, drawn from different model families and excluding whichever assembled this object. Every signalling question answer is published in the supplement. Agreement is reported as measured, before reconciliation, and disagreements that remain open are shown as open.
Certainty and robustness

Certainty was rated with GRADE. Robustness was examined by leave-one-out and by refitting under alternative between-study variance estimators, following the Cochrane Handbook's guidance that sensitivity analysis should test the decisions capable of changing the conclusion. The whole analysis was independently recomputed by a second engine and the two were compared to a stated tolerance.

blocks.text: Study selection

423 records were screened and 4 trials met all four eligibility conditions, contributing 9,734 randomised participants. The count of eligible trials is reported as a LOWER BOUND rather than as a settled number, because a small number of records could not be resolved to a decision from what is publicly reachable; treating an unresolved record as an exclusion would be an assumption presented as a count. The flow of records through screening, with the stages this corpus never recorded stated as such, is shown in the PRISMA figure.
Trial characteristics

The 4 trials differ in ways that matter for interpretation. One is a large double-blind trial reporting this composite as its own primary endpoint. Two enrolled chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy, one of them open-label with blinded adjudication and reporting this composite behind a win-ratio primary. One is double-blind and small. Characteristics are in Table 1 and per-arm counts in Table 2. Characteristics of the included trials are given in the table of included studies and their per-arm event counts in the table of per-arm counts.
Primary synthesis

The pooled hazard ratio was 0.872 (0.746 to 1.02, 95% interval), favouring sacubitril/valsartan over enalapril. Between-trial heterogeneity was low: I-squared 32.9%, tau-squared 0.0086, with Q of 5.16 on 3 degrees of freedom. The individual estimates range from 0.8 to 1.83, and that spread is real even though the heterogeneity statistics are small, because three of the four intervals include the null and two of those span more than a doubling of risk. The per-trial and pooled estimates are shown in the forest plot. The prediction interval for a future study runs from 0.686 to 1.11.
Robustness

The pooled result is not robust to the removal of the largest trial. Omitting it gives 0.966 (0.79 to 1.18), an interval that includes the null. The three smaller trials are therefore individually and jointly compatible with no effect on this composite, and the pooled estimate is best read as the large trial's result, slightly attenuated by the three smaller trials, which neither confirm nor contradict it. Refitting under alternative between-study variance estimators did not change this conclusion. Each refit is shown in the leave-one-out figure and tabulated in the leave-one-out table; 2 of 4 refits still exclude no difference.
Cross-engine verification

The whole synthesis was recomputed independently and the two engines agreed on the point estimate and both bounds to within the stated tolerance, with Q and its degrees of freedom matching exactly. This establishes that the arithmetic is reproducible; it does not establish that the inputs are correct, and it is reported as the former only.
Risk of bias

No domain in any trial was rated at high risk of bias by either assessor. The two assessors agreed on 10/15 domain judgements (66.7%), and on 1 of 3 overall judgements. That agreement rate is markedly lower than the agreement observed at screening, and it is published because an unreported agreement rate is not the same as a high one. Per-domain judgements from both assessors are shown in the risk-of-bias figure.
Certainty of the evidence

GRADE certainty for this outcome is low, downgraded for risk of bias and for imprecision. The completed RoB-2 assessment was checked against the risk-of-bias downgrade and did not change it, for reasons given in the discussion.
Subgroup analysis

One subgroup analysis was performed and it was NOT pre-specified. Splitting the pool by aetiology gives 0.838 (0.675 to 1.04) across the 2 trials in unrestricted heart failure and 1.11 (0.598 to 2.05) across the 2 trials restricted to Chagas cardiomyopathy. The test for interaction returns p = 0.538 and a ratio of hazard ratios of 1.16 (0.717 to 1.89), so the difference between the strata is compatible with chance. Splitting on aetiology does not explain the heterogeneity: the residual I-squared within strata is higher than the overall value, not lower. Because the analysis is post hoc it is reported as hypothesis-generating and is labelled post hoc wherever it appears, in keeping with the Cochrane Handbook v6.5 section 10.11.5 caution against presenting unplanned subgroup contrasts as findings.
Small-study effects

A funnel plot is shown and Egger's regression test was run for completeness, returning an intercept of -0.3 with p = 0.0106. Neither is interpreted. At 4 trials the Cochrane Handbook v6.5 section 13.3.5.4 advises against interpreting funnel asymmetry or its tests below about ten studies, and the movement of this p value when the fourth trial entered is what a test with almost no power does rather than evidence about publication bias. No claim about small-study effects is made in either direction.
Comparison with published syntheses

One published synthesis on the same comparison had a readable included-study table and was reconciled against this review trial by trial. 13 checks were applied to it, of which 9 came back clean, 2 identified an error and 2 identified a reporting item that is absent. Its included-study list is also the reason this review's k rose during the build: PARALLEL-HF was eligible on every axis of the frozen question, was absent from the brief this object was built from, and was recovered from that list, verified against its own publication and registry record, and pooled. The full reconciliation, the quoted evidence for every check with its location, and the decomposition of where the two reviews differ are given in the section on comparison with published syntheses.

Almost no published review reports its RoB-2 inter-assessor agreement at all, so there is no external benchmark. We publish it because an unreported agreement rate is not the same as a high one.

blocks.text: Integrity flag. assessor 1 cited a statistical analysis plan by version number and release date 'PARACHUTE-HF SAP version 2.1, release date 29-Apr-2025' appears in assessor 1's D1 and D2 sources, and it marked protocol_available true for those domains. That specificity was not in the packet we supplied. It is either a genuine retrieval or a recalled identifier, and the output alone cannot tell us which. NOT adopted. Any domain resting on it is treated as protocol-unavailable until the SAP is retrieved and checked. This is the identifier-from-recall failure mode this project has already been caught by once.

Effect on the GRADE risk-of-bias rating: it does NOT move. It was serious before the assessment and remains serious. Two reasons, and the second is the load-bearing one.

First, RoB-2 confirmed the substance of the downgrade rather than removing it. Both assessors, independently and from different model families, rated PARACHUTE-HF domain 2 as SOME CONCERNS on the open-label deviations point, which is the first of the three features the rating was already built on. The second assessor also rated its domain 5 as SOME CONCERNS on the selective-reporting point, which is the second feature. The assessment agreed with the reasoning the rating rested on.

Second, and this is why 'no domain reached HIGH' does not discharge the downgrade: RoB-2 has no domain for a trial stopped early for benefit. Early stopping is not a randomization failure, a deviation, missing data, a measurement problem, or selective reporting of a result; it is a stopping-rule effect on the magnitude of the estimate, and the RoB-2 tool does not ask about it in any of its five domains. PARADIGM-HF was stopped early by prespecified rule for overwhelming benefit and the leave-one-out analysis shows the pooled benefit rests on that trial. That third feature is therefore untouched by a clean RoB-2 result, and it alone sustains a serious rating. Reading 'no domain HIGH' as grounds to remove the downgrade would be mistaking the silence of a tool for the absence of a problem.

The opposite reading is available and is recorded here rather than suppressed: under a common mapping, trials at SOME CONCERNS with none at HIGH support 'not serious', which would raise certainty from low to moderate. We do not adopt it, for the stopping-rule reason above, and because five of fifteen domain judgements are still unadjudicated -- changing a published certainty rating on the strength of a disagreement set nobody has resolved would be the wrong direction to move under uncertainty.

Our own multi-source extraction pass did not record this discrepancy at all. A blinded comparator found it. The two sources disagree on both numerator and denominator for the same quantity in the same trial, and we carried only one side without noticing the other existed. Recorded here with both values and both pointers rather than resolved, because resolving it requires reading which population and which window each source is reporting, and picking one now would manufacture the appearance of a resolution. A multi-source pass that agrees with itself is not the same as a pass that checked both sources. This is the class our own harness names as 'consistency does not authenticate a row'.
Comparison with published syntheses

Every paper this project ships carries this section. A synthesis that reports only its own result asks a reader to take the field on trust; one that reconciles itself against the published syntheses on the same question, names what they got right as prominently as what they got wrong, and shows the denominator, can be checked. The classes applied below are the classes this review must itself survive. On the night this section was written, this object failed three of them: analysis panels computed at k=3 under a k=4 headline, a title stating a study count its own contents contradicted, and a figure labelled as a diagnostic it was not drawing.

By lookup, never recall. The comparison review's identifiers were resolved through the PubMed ID converter on 2026-08-14: DOI 10.7759/cureus.48623 returns PMID 38084196 and PMCID PMC10710849. Its full text is staged in this bundle and every quotation below was read from that file.

1,066 retrieved, 985 screened after duplicates, 28 full texts, nine included. Monotone decreasing and internally consistent; no stage exceeds the one above it.
Whether their omission of PARACHUTE-HF is an error or a date

Their search closed 15 September 2023. PARACHUTE-HF reported in 2026. Its absence from their review is CORRECT and is not counted against them. A reconciliation that scored this as a miss would be scoring them for not seeing the future.
Whether including a retrospective cohort breaches their OWN stated eligibility

It does not. Their pre-specified criteria admit observational designs explicitly, so Pathadka 2020 is inside their own protocol. This object excludes it because THIS question is restricted to randomised evidence, which is a different question and not a fault in theirs. Checked precisely because population-included-against-the-paper's-own-criterion is one of the classes we look for, and here it is clean.
Whether the influential non-randomised study was tested

It was, and the result is reported in the body rather than buried: removing Pathadka moves all-cause mortality from 0.57 to 0.85 and heterogeneity from 94 per cent to 0. Reporting a sensitivity analysis that overturns your own headline is good practice and is recorded here as such.
Absence of a funnel plot or small-study test

None is reported, and at nine studies none is expected: the Cochrane Handbook advises against interpreting these tests below about ten. Their omission is defensible and is NOT counted as a defect. This object applies the same caution to its own Egger's test at k = 4.
Whether the Discussion's significance claim matches the primary estimate

The primary all-cause mortality estimate is RR 0.57 with a 95 per cent interval of 0.31 to 1.04. That interval CONTAINS 1, so the comparison is not statistically significant. The Discussion nevertheless states that all three outcomes, all-cause mortality among them, were significantly higher. The statement is true of their RCT-only sensitivity result, 0.85 (0.78 to 0.93), and is not true of the analysis the abstract leads with. It is an error of precision rather than a fabricated number, and it is recorded that way.
Whether the abstract's headline carries the heterogeneity it rests on

The abstract reports RR 0.57 (0.31 to 1.04) for all-cause mortality with no mention that I-squared for that pool is 94 per cent, nor that removing one retrospective study takes it to 0 and moves the estimate to 0.85. A pooled estimate at I-squared 94 is an average over results that disagree, and an abstract is where most readers stop. Their own body text is transparent about both facts; the abstract is not.

No Cochrane RoB, Jadad, Newcastle-Ottawa or equivalent appears anywhere in the text. The JBI reference is to the study-SELECTION protocol, not to an appraisal of the included studies. Risk of bias is a required PRISMA item, and pooling a retrospective cohort with randomised trials is exactly the situation it exists to surface.

PROSPERO is not mentioned and no registration of any kind is stated, so the analysis cannot be checked against a pre-specified plan. Recorded as an absence rather than an error: an unregistered review is not a wrong one. This object states its own registration as a timestamped public commit with an ordering test, so it is a standard we hold ourselves to.

blocks.text: Where our result differs from theirs
This review: HR 0.872 (0.746 to 1.018) for cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalisation, k=4, time-to-first-event.
That review: RR 0.76 (0.66 to 0.86) for cardiovascular hospitalisation and RR 0.75 (0.62 to 0.91) for cardiovascular mortality, reported as separate outcomes.

Four reasons, none of which is an error by either side: a different estimand (hazard of a FIRST event against risk over whole follow-up); a different eligible set (they admit observational designs, we do not); a different search window (ours includes two trials published after theirs closed); and a different composite (they report hospitalisation and cardiovascular death separately, we pool the composite of the two). Decomposed rather than asserting ours is right: on the trials and the quantity the two reviews share, they agree.
Statistical output, quoted verbatim

Every result below carries the VERBATIM printed output of the call that produced it, captured with capture.output() rather than re-typed. A bare number can only be checked against the object that produced it, and the object is ours; a quoted metafor call carries its own k, its own estimator, its own heterogeneity and its own package version, so a reader can audit the provenance without trusting us. It would have made this project's worst defect visible on sight: a printed k = 4 sitting under a leave-one-out panel drawn from three studies is obvious, where a bare 0.839 is not.

The quoted output is parsed and compared against the projected values at the moment it is stored -- k, I-squared, Q and the back-transformed estimate with its interval. A quotation that disagrees with the number printed beside it is worse than no quotation, because it looks like provenance. The write refuses if they disagree.

blocks.text: Discussion
Principal findings

Across 4 randomised trials and 9,734 participants, the pooled hazard of a first cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation with sacubitril/valsartan relative to enalapril was 0.872 (0.746 to 1.02), an interval that includes no difference, with a pooled hazard ratio of 0.872 (0.746 to 1.02). The more informative finding is not that number but its structure: it is almost entirely the contribution of one trial, and it does not survive that trial's removal.
Interpreting the estimate

A pooled hazard ratio of 0.872 on this composite is a clinically meaningful reduction if it is real, but the interval does not exclude the null: it runs from 0.746 to 1.018. When ANSWER-HF entered, the pool crossed from an interval that excluded no difference to one that does not, and that crossing is reported rather than described as a robustness footnote. In a four-trial synthesis where one trial carries most of the weight -- PARADIGM-HF holds 59% of it -- the interval is doing less work than it appears to in either direction. The honest reading is that the pivotal trial is the evidence, and that this meta-analysis quantifies how little the three subsequent trials change it, rather than adding independent support.
Heterogeneity

I-squared of 32.9% falls in the band conventionally described as low, and tau-squared is 0.0086. It would be a mistake to read that as agreement between the trials. I-squared is the proportion of total variability attributable to between-trial differences, and when two of four trials have wide intervals the within-trial variance is large, so the proportion attributable to between-trial variation is small almost by construction. The point estimates range from 0.8 to 1.83, which spans a clinically important reduction and essentially no effect. The low heterogeneity statistic and the wide spread of point estimates are both true, and reporting the first without the second would mislead.
The leave-one-out finding

Removing the largest trial moves the pooled estimate to 0.966 (0.79 to 1.18). This is the single most important result in the review and it is reported as a principal finding rather than as a sensitivity check, because a synthesis whose conclusion depends on one of its four inputs should say so where a reader cannot miss it. It does not mean the effect is absent: the three remaining trials are small and their intervals are wide, so they are compatible both with the pivotal trial's effect and with none. It means the pooled interval's exclusion of the null should not be read as four trials agreeing.
Why the risk-of-bias rating did not change

The completed RoB-2 assessment found no domain at high risk in any trial, which might be taken as grounds to remove the GRADE risk-of-bias downgrade. It was not, for a reason worth stating plainly: RoB-2 has no domain for a trial stopped early for benefit. Early stopping is not a randomisation failure, a deviation from intended intervention, missing outcome data, a measurement problem, or selective reporting of a result. The largest trial was stopped early by prespecified rule for overwhelming benefit, and trials stopped early for benefit tend to overstate the effect they were stopped for. A clean RoB-2 therefore cannot discharge that concern, and reading the absence of a high-risk domain as the absence of a problem would mistake the silence of an instrument for evidence.
Comparison with other evidence

This review reconciles itself against the one published synthesis on this comparison whose included-study table could be read, trial by trial, and reports the checks applied to it with their denominator in the section on comparison with published syntheses. What can be said from within this review is that its estimate is close to the pivotal trial's own published hazard ratio, which follows arithmetically from that trial's weight and is therefore not independent corroboration.
Strengths

The protocol was registered before the first query with a machine-checkable ordering test. Every screened record is published with its disposition. Both risk-of-bias assessors' full answers are published unreconciled, with the agreement rate as measured. Every number on every surface is projected from one canonical object, so the manuscript, the tables, the figures and the web page cannot disagree with one another. A disagreement between two sources that this review's own extraction missed is published as an unresolved disagreement rather than silently resolved.
Limitations
The synthesis rests on 4 trials, one of which contributes most of the weight, and the pooled result does not survive its removal. This is stated as a principal finding rather than a caveat.

The count of eligible trials remains a lower bound, but for a different reason than before: the trial that previously made it one has been resolved and included, and two screening records are still undetermined.
Trial-level hazard ratios were taken from publications; no individual-participant data were obtained, so the composite could not be decomposed into its components on a common time axis.

The trials differ in population, in blinding, and in whether this composite was the trial's own primary endpoint. Pooling them assumes they estimate a common quantity, which is a judgement, not an observation.

Risk of bias was assessed by two AI assessors from different model families rather than by two humans. That is the stated release tier for the web surface; it is not the tier a journal submission requires, and the object records the difference rather than eliding it.
Five of fifteen risk-of-bias domain judgements remain unadjudicated. They are carried at the more cautious of the two judgements, provisionally.

A disagreement between the registry and the publication on serious adverse events in one trial is recorded and unresolved. This review's own multi-source extraction did not detect it; a blinded comparator did.

Omitting PARADIGM-HF gives 0.9660 (0.7897 to 1.1818) with I-squared falling to 1.2%. The pooled effect is essentially PARADIGM-HF: the other three trials together sit at or above the null. Omitting ANSWER-HF returns exactly the previous 0.8392 (0.7429 to 0.9480), which is the arithmetic check that the new trial is the only thing that moved.

The one apparent gap this search had is now closed, and closing it removed a trial rather than adding one: the patient total of the paywalled Chagas reviews exceeded the trials found here by a post hoc PARADIGM-HF subgroup, which is not a separate randomisation and is not recovered. The reconciliation block sets out the arithmetic and the deduplication reason. What is still unread is how those reviews themselves treated that subgroup, which their abstracts do not say.

The protocol commit precedes the first executed query on both readings of 'first query'. The 12:19:18Z attempt is reported even though it returned nothing, because reporting only the successful execution would move the first-query time three minutes later and make the claim look better than it is. This is the test a PROSPERO record cannot offer: the timestamps are set by the repository and by the APIs, not by us, and both are independently checkable.

Computed at BUILD time by metafor 5.0.1 under R 4.6.0 from the per-arm 2x2 counts stored on each trial, which were READ from the sources named on each cell. No composite was reconstructed by addition and no count was derived from a percentage. The L'Abbe panel was therefore drawing three points beside a four-trial forest. Conclusions

In adults with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction, the pooled hazard of a first cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation with sacubitril/valsartan compared with enalapril was 0.872 (0.746 to 1.02) at low certainty, an interval consistent with no difference. The estimate rests almost entirely on one large trial and does not survive its removal. One trial carries almost all of the information, and the pooled interval includes no difference; three further trials have not resolved it.
Sections not written, and why

Formal comparison with previous meta-analyses. This review's search was designed to find randomised trials reporting the estimand, not to find previous syntheses. Writing a comparison would require either a second search that was not run or recall of literature that was not retrieved, and recalled literature is the failure mode this project has already been caught by once.
